# 54 Definition and Classification of Pancreatitis


1. The first consensus meeting that tried to separate acute from chronic pancreatitis solely on morphologic grounds was held in  
A. Atlanta  
B. Cambridge  
**C. Marseille 1963**  
D. Rome 1988  
E. Zurich 1997  

2. According to Lagerlof (1942), the key historic step in pancreatitis nomenclature was distinguishing  
A. Alcoholic vs gallstone pancreatitis  
B. Interstitial vs necrotising forms  
**C. Acute pancreatitis from chronic pancreatitis**  
D. Mild vs severe attacks  
E. Obstructive vs calcific disease  

3. The inability to obtain pancreatic tissue during life led past classifications to rely mainly on  
A. Genetic testing  
B. Animal models  
**C. Clinical, morphologic and laboratory features**  
D. Autopsy series only  
E. Serum IgG4 levels  

4. Recurrent acute pancreatitis is considered the best example of  
A. Autoimmune pancreatitis  
B. Post-operative pancreatitis  
**C. The continuum between acute and chronic disease**  
D. Obstructive chronic pancreatitis  
E. Tropical calcific pancreatitis  

5. The Cambridge 1984 meeting abandoned the term  
A. Acute pancreatitis  
B. Chronic pancreatitis  
**C. Relapsing pancreatitis**  
D. Pseudocyst  
E. Phlegmon  

6. In the Cambridge classification, morphologic changes in chronic pancreatitis were best demonstrated by  
A. Serum amylase  
B. PET-CT  
**C. ERCP**  
D. Endoscopic ultrasound only  
E. Laparoscopy  

7. ERCP ductal changes are NON-specific because similar alterations can be seen in  
A. Only autoimmune pancreatitis  
B. Only pancreatic cancer  
**C. Cholelithiasis, Sjögren’s, sclerosing cholangitis**  
D. Only tropical pancreatitis  
E. Only hereditary pancreatitis  

8. The 1984 Revised Marseille meeting added which new entity?  
A. Mild acute pancreatitis  
B. Post-necrotic pseudocyst  
**C. Obstructive chronic pancreatitis**  
D. Autoimmune pancreatitis  
E. Groove pancreatitis  

9. Obstructive chronic pancreatitis is typically  
A. Irreversible even after relieving obstruction  
B. Always accompanied by IgG4 elevation  
**C. Proximal duct dilation secondary to downstream stricture or tumour**  
D. A form of acute necrotising pancreatitis  
E. Confined to the pancreatic tail

A. Always permanent  
B. Always calcific  
**C. Reversible in almost half of patients**  
D. Indicative of autoimmune disease  
E. Synonymous with chronic inflammatory pancreatitis

B. An ERCP-based grading  
**C. A clinically-based, dynamic system**  
D. Purely histologic

B. An infected pseudocyst  
**C. An inflammatory mass in/around the pancreas**  
D. A sterile fluid collection with a wall

A. Covers all aetiologies equally  
B. Requires IgG4 staining  
C. Is pediatric-oriented  
**D. Focuses on alcoholic chronic pancreatitis**

B. Interstitial, necrotising, haemorrhagic  
**C. Definite vs probable**  
D. Type 1 vs Type 2 autoimmune

A. Only imaging findings  
B. Only post-operative cases  
**C. Risk factors / aetiology**  
D. Only paediatric patients

B. Age  
**C. Autoimmune**

B. Complications  
C. Functional insufficiency  
**D. Serum IgG4 level**

18. Manchester system classifies pain control by

B. Monthly opioids  
**C. Weekly opiates**  
D. Yearly steroids  
E. No analgesia needed  

19. End-stage Manchester chronic pancreatitis MUST include  
A. Acute attacks only  
B. IgG4 > 2× upper limit  
**C. Extrapancreatic features (biliary stricture, duodenal stenosis, etc.)**

20. M-ANNHEIM scoring assigns the HIGHEST points to  
A. Mild pain  
B. Steatorrhoea only  
C. Transient organ failure  
**D. Endocrine insufficiency / diabetes**

21. Revised Atlanta 2012 defines severe acute pancreatitis by  
A. CT severity index > 6  
B. Any peripancreatic fluid  
C. Amylase > 3× ULN  
**D. Persistent organ failure > 48 h**  
E. Need for ERCP  

22. Determinant-based classification uses two main mortality determinants: persistent organ failure and  
A. Serum Ca²⁺ < 1.8 mmol/L  
B. Body mass index > 30  
**C. Infected (peri)pancreatic necrosis**  
D. Pseudocyst diameter > 6 cm  
E. Need for surgery

A. Transient organ failure  
B. Sterile necrosis only  
**C. Infected necrosis plus persistent organ failure**  
D. No necrosis but severe pain
